Nowy Dwor Mazowiecki Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Nowy Dwór Mazowiecki, Poland

Not demolished. Jews are first recorded in Nowy Dwór in the 16th century, though the community developed significantly only post-partition; by 1921, 3,916 (50%) were mostly killed by Germans in 1942. This cemetery's precise founding remains debated - historian Ignacy Schiper claimed it predated 1780, though demographic and cartographic evidence casts doubt on an 18th-century origin, with the first confirmed record appearing in an 1829 regional synagogue-district register. It served Jews from Nowy Dwór and surrounding villages, including Jabłonna, Nieporęt, Wieliszew, and Zegrze, with a funeral house and at least one ohel present by the early 20th century. Holocaust victims and execution victims were buried here during WWII; Poland formally closed the cemetery on May 24, 1962. Postwar sand mining and tombstone theft continued for decades; a 1994 partial hill leveling designated part of the land for development. In 2010-2011, local Jews fenced the site and arranged a lapidary from recovered town tombstones.
